name: Victor Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What fills a normal day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I direct the choir at a parish church, play organ for services and lead a four-player wedding group. I have a music master's and can coax a rough choir into tune, but the parish pays a low fixed fee for all that preparation.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does the family manage around those hours?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Ruth works at a bakery, and our two children are in school. We have a mortgage and about three weeks of expenses saved; there are only a couple of paid choir posts within a sensible drive. I've never used AI. I keep the service book and player calls on paper.

say: I'd ask for **written wedding deposits** before celebrating faster messages.
I'd tell the choir **rehearsal time** needs paying even with better office tools.
think: Our **three-week reserve** cannot handle a cancelled wedding and a short bakery week together.
I have **never used AI**, and small automation would not repair the parish's low fee.
do: Get **service calls** and two wedding dates signed this week.
Pause the children's **paid football club** for a month if a wedding deposit fails.
feel: I feel **anxious** because one cancelled Saturday can reach essential bills.
S0.quote: A full diary with no deposit can still leave a family short on Monday.
fieldNote: His **choir leadership** and master's coexist with low fixed pay and only three weeks saved.
A cancelled **wedding deposit** has already forced a short family loan for groceries.

steps.text: Get next parish service calls and two wedding dates signed
Pause paid football club one month if wedding deposit fails

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the wedding players that faster booking messages are fine, provided the agreed fee still comes through. The choir cannot rehearse on an unpaid promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little office automation would leave the organ and the singers where they are, but our income is already tight. Three weeks saved will not cover a cancelled wedding and a short bakery week together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll ask the parish to sign the next month's service calls and confirm the wedding group's two booked Saturdays. If one wedding cancels without its deposit, Ruth and I will pause the children's paid football club for a month before touching the mortgage payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the ordinary calendar even in a quiet AI world. One lost Saturday is already too close to the food bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened after a wedding cancellation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A couple cancelled in spring after I had held the Saturday, and the deposit terms were only spoken. We borrowed grocery money from Ruth's sister and repaid it when the next service fee arrived.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you avoid that next time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I now ask for deposits in writing before turning down another wedding date. A full diary with no deposit can still leave a family short on Monday.

say: I'd ask for a **written rehearsal rate** before software changes the parish fee.
I'd discuss **paid preparation** directly with the council treasurer.
think: About **one-quarter of my pay** from preparation could shrink.
Three weeks saved makes a **lasting fee cut** impossible for the household.
do: Compare **twelve weeks of preparation** with the parish fee and request a written rate this month.
Offer **extra choir practice** after lost fees only with signed teaching fee, written room cost and ten paying singers.
Keep **current services and weddings**; refund deposits if the hall date fails.
feel: I feel **alarmed** because even a quarter-pay loss could outrun our reserve.
S1.quote: I would rather bargain for an honest rate than pretend I can replace the parish overnight.
fieldNote: He negotiates **directly with the parish** for paid preparation instead of assuming another local choir job exists.
His **extra practice** requires written pay, hall terms and ten committed singers; he has never tried AI.

steps.text: Request written rehearsal rate using twelve weeks of preparation records
Offer extra practice after fee loss with signed teaching fee, room cost and ten paying singers
Keep current services and weddings; refund deposits if hall fails

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the parish council which paid arrangement and booking work it plans to hand to software. I would sit down with the treasurer and insist the new service fee include rehearsal hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Arrangements, practice sheets and booking make about a quarter of my pay. I expect those hours to be priced out first, and we cannot lose even a quarter for long with three weeks saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll put twelve weeks of choir preparation beside the parish fee and ask for a written rehearsal rate. In the first year of change, if preparation fees fall, I'll offer another paid choir practice only if the parish signs my rate, provides the room and at least ten singers commit to a term fee. I'll keep the existing services and wedding dates while that is decided.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because a quarter-pay loss would hit before we rebuild savings. I would rather bargain for an honest rate than pretend I can replace the parish overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the parish hall free for that extra practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hall is used by a youth group on Thursdays, so it is not mine to promise. I will ask the council for a written room date and fee before inviting singers; if the room falls through, I will refund deposits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the practice-sheet maker?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The organist at another parish offered to show me an AI practice-sheet maker. I have never used one; I would watch a live demonstration and check every note against the score before considering it, with written permission for any singer recording.

say: I'd seek **signed service fees** before AGI changes paid arrangements.
I'd tell singers **robot organists** follow thinking AGI by about three years.
think: **AGI in 2028** could erase preparation fees before robot players arrive around 2031.
Our **three-week reserve** cannot cover a quarter-pay loss in a town with few vacancies.
do: List **three income streams** and request signed parish hours now.
Apply **after 2028** if preparation fees halve, only for a posted qualifying director job with pickup and written replacement net pay.
Keep **current services and weddings** until offer; ask lender for written total interest before arrears if paid services also fall.
feel: I feel **alarmed** because fee loss could outrun three weeks of savings and scarce jobs.
S2.quote: An empty church noticeboard is not an open job.
fieldNote: His **2028 planning loss** arrives before robot organ playing around 2031.
His **job application** depends on a posted vacancy, recognised master's, pickup and written net pay after travel.

steps.text: Keep services/weddings until signed offer; list income and request written parish hours
Apply after 2028 if fees halve and posted director role accepts master's
Require pickup and written net pay after travel before leaving services or weddings
Ask lender before arrears if services fall; review written total added interest before accepting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the singers that AGI by 2028 could write arrangements before robots can play organ around 2031. I would get the next service and wedding fees on paper immediately.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paid planning could vanish quickly while the choir still needs a director in the room. With three weeks saved and only a few nearby posts, a quarter-pay loss could put the mortgage behind before I find another contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll separate service, wedding and teaching pay and ask the parish for next season's signed hours. In the first year after 2028, if preparation fees halve, I'll apply for a posted music-director job in the next district only if my master's qualifies, the timetable fits school pickup and its written net pay after travel replaces the loss. I will keep present services and booked weddings until another offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about losing fees faster than we can earn them back. An empty church noticeboard is not an open job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a music-director opening now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The next district hired a director last year and the post is filled. I'll ask when another is advertised, but I won't tell Ruth to count that wage yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if paid services also fall?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the parish also cuts paid services, Ruth and I will ask our lender about temporary terms before arrears. We'll get the total added interest in writing before accepting anything.

say: I'd ask for **written player rates** and wedding deposits.
I'd stage a **parish concert** only after sponsor, hall and ticket conditions are met.
think: **AGI in 2031** threatens booking before robot players follow around 2034.
**Planning pay** could fade sooner, leaving no room for unpaid live experiments.
do: Agree **written player rates** before posting names; add deposit deadlines to wedding quotes this season.
Stage a **parish concert** after arranging loss only with cleared sponsor, written hall insurance, inspected organ and twelve prepaid tickets covering players.
Repeat **after 2031** only with renewed sponsor, written hall terms, agreed rates and twelve tickets; refund if eight sell.
feel: I feel **alarmed** because planning fees may fall before a funded concert exists.
S3.quote: A provisional hall date is not a contract for the players.
fieldNote: His **concert plan** requires cleared sponsor money, insurance, written hall terms and paid four-player group rates before publicity.
His **ticket floor** protects the family reserve by cancelling and refunding an underfilled show.

steps.text: Quote written wedding player rates and deposit deadlines
Clear sponsor funds, sign hall insurance, inspect organ and show player rates before poster
Stage after arranging loss only with twelve prepaid tickets covering players; refund eight buyers if short
Repeat after 2031 only with renewed sponsor, signed hall insurance, agreed rates and twelve paid tickets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell wedding couples we have five years to write fair deposits and player rates into contracts. The players should see their fee before their names go on a poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2031 could write the arrangements and book the four-player group, while robot players might follow around 2034. Ordinary tools could trim the planning pay much sooner, so another live date needs to pay everyone rather than create more unpaid preparation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This season I'll put player rates and a deposit deadline into every new wedding quote. By 2031, if arranging fees fall, I'll propose a separate parish concert only if a sponsor's money has cleared for room and insurance, the hall signs its terms and twelve tickets are prepaid to cover the four-player group. In the first year after AGI, I'll repeat it only if the sponsor renews, hall insurance remains signed, players accept written rates and twelve paid tickets still cover them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed that planning pay could fall before a new concert pays. I cannot put the household's mortgage money into a poster and hope people come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the hall is provisional or only eight tickets sell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The parish has offered a possible hall date, not a signed room. Players will see their written rates before I advertise; if only eight tickets sell, I'll refund them and keep the booked wedding work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who checks the hall and instrument safety?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before a poster goes up, I would check hall insurance and require its technician to inspect and secure the organ. A provisional hall date is not a contract for the players.

say: I'd ask for a **paid apprenticeship** with signed teaching and safe-room terms.
I'd keep **current services** until another choir signs actual pay.
think: At **53 in 2036**, I still need wages for the mortgage.
**Arrangement fees** may thin earlier, with robot players following around 2039.
do: Seek a **paid organ apprenticeship** only with signed teaching fee, room and safeguards for young players.
Build **two months' savings** from cleared extra wedding fees after players and essential bills by 2036.
Apply **after 2036** if preparation fees fall, only for a posted qualifying choir job with pickup and signed mortgage-covering net pay.
feel: I feel **anxious** because a long warning does not pay today's bills.
S4.quote: A young player's training should not be another unpaid hour on my bill.
fieldNote: His **apprenticeship idea** reflects family and community ties but requires an approved budget and safe supervised room.
His **savings goal** uses only paid extra weddings after player pay and essential bills, never unbooked hopes.

steps.text: Start organ apprenticeship only with signed council fee, room and youth safeguards
Save cleared extra-wedding surplus after players, mortgage, electricity and food toward two months by 2036
Apply after 2036 if fees fall and posted choir role accepts master's
Keep services until signed full-time offer with pickup and net-after-travel pay covering mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the parish that ten years allows a proper apprenticeship for young players, provided the tutor is paid. I would ask the council for a signed training fee rather than a thank-you speech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 53 in 2036 and still paying the mortgage; robot players might reach services around 2039. Arrangement fees could go much earlier, so a decade of warning does not solve this month's shortage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll ask the council to fund a paid organ apprenticeship and confirm both the church's fee and a safe rehearsal slot in writing. By 2036 I'll try to save two months of expenses from cleared extra wedding fees after player pay, mortgage, electricity and food are covered. In the first year after AGI, if parish preparation fees fall, I'll apply for a posted full-time choir post only if my master's qualifies, pickup works and a signed net offer after travel covers the mortgage; I'll keep current services until then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the longer path, because I can ask for pay now but cannot make another parish hire me. A young player's training should not be another unpaid hour on my bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has the council funded an apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The council likes the apprenticeship idea but has approved no budget. I will not invite a trainee until it signs the teaching fee, room time and safeguarding arrangements for young players.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would two months of savings come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The two extra weddings I hope for are not booked yet. I will move money to savings only after deposits and final fees clear and essential bills are paid.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because arrangement fees could fall before another parish offers paid work. Signed service calls, a real qualifying vacancy and written lender costs if services also shrink would help us keep the mortgage paid.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who pays a choir leader for preparing music after the children are asleep. The last bar of music can still be an unpaid hour of work.

headlineQuote: The last bar of music can still be an unpaid hour of work.
portrait: Victor is a **43-year-old choir director** with a music master's, partner, two children and a mortgage.
Despite **senior skill**, he earns little, has three weeks saved and few nearby choir openings.
He has **never used AI** and would require a live demonstration, manual checks and recording permission before considering it.
He seeks **paid preparation** and safely funded live work before leaving current services for a written offer.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** could remove arranging fees before another paid parish role appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed service calls**, a posted qualifying role and full lender costs would protect mortgage payments.
